name: Timekeeping and Billing Narratives
title: Timekeeping and Billing Narratives
answer: Timekeeping and billing narratives cover the written descriptions that lawyers and paralegals attach to billable time, along with the systems and rules that turn those entries into client invoices. The scope includes task and activity codes, matter budgets, outside counsel guidelines, e-billing submissions, and the review of entries for clarity, accuracy, and compliance. It also touches alternative fee arrangements, because narratives may be used to justify value rather than only hours. In legal operations, the topic sits between practice management, finance, and client service, and it is increasingly shaped by tools that draft or check narrative text.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These workflows run on time and billing platforms, practice management systems, matter management tools, and e-billing hubs that exchange data in formats such as LEDES. Identity and access controls decide who can see, edit, or approve time entries, and audit logs record changes for later review. AI features may run in the vendor cloud or inside a firm's own environment, drawing on calendars, documents, emails, and prior entries. Security controls include encryption, role-based permissions, retention rules, and separation between client matters. The infrastructure must also preserve the link between an original time record and any AI-assisted revision.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts with time capture, whether by timer, calendar review, or manual entry, and then moves to narrative writing. AI can suggest a first draft from matter context, document activity, or meeting notes, and it can flag vague phrases, block billing, or entries that fall outside client guidelines. Reviewers compare the narrative to the underlying work, edit for accuracy, and approve the entry before it reaches an invoice. Evaluation often uses sample entries, rule sets, and feedback from billing attorneys and clients. The method is human in the loop, because a plausible sentence is not the same as a true record of work.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on fee reasonableness, client consent, confidentiality, privilege, and the accuracy of the record. A narrative that overstates work, hides a clerical task, or invents detail can create billing disputes, ethics complaints, or claims of fraud. Provenance matters, so firms should be able to show what was written by a person, what was suggested by a model, and what source data supported the entry. Client outside counsel guidelines and e-billing rules may require disclosure of AI use, prohibit certain charges, or demand detailed task descriptions. Data used to train or prompt a model must respect client confidentiality and the firm's obligations to protect matter information.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward less manual time capture, with passive tools that infer activity from calendars, documents, and communications, and toward narratives that are drafted and checked in real time. Firms and clients are likely to expect clearer standards for AI-assisted entries, including labels, audit trails, and rules for what can be billed. Analytics may compare narratives against budgets, guidelines, and historical patterns to spot outliers before submission. As clients push for value and transparency, billing narratives may become shorter, more structured, and more closely tied to matter outcomes. Regulation and case law will continue to shape how much automation is acceptable in the billing record.
